---
title: "Understanding the Math"
---

The [Algorithm](algorithm.qmd) pages walk through *what* the SHREC pipeline
computes, stage by stage. This section is the companion *why*: the handful of
mathematical ideas that make each stage work, the conventions that are easy to
get subtly wrong, and the reasoning that pins each piece as correct.

It grew out of a working journal kept while building the math-correctness test
suite (`docs/tests-math.md`, the `MM<n>` oracles) — every subtlety here was
either a design decision, a bug that the tests caught, or a "why is it done
*this* way" question that turned out to have a real answer.

## A map of the pipeline to the ideas

| Pipeline stage | The deep questions | Page |
|---|---|---|
| **2. Adaptive kernel** | Why `log₂ M`? Why subtract the nearest-neighbour distance? Why a *bracketed* root-solve? What is the fuzzy-union symmetrisation really doing? | [The adaptive kernel](explainer-kernel.qmd) |
| **4. Reconstruction** | Why the Fiedler eigenvector of `L = D − A`? What does eigenvalue 0 count? RatioCut vs NCut, and degenerate eigenspaces. | [From graph to driver](explainer-spectral.qmd) |
| **3. Consensus** | Why *mean* the per-response graphs? Power means and the min↔mean↔max dial. How adding data drives a *percolation transition*. | [Pooling & percolation](explainer-consensus.qmd) |
| **End to end** | What can SHREC provably recover, and what can't it? Invariances, phase-vs-value, and the representational limit. | [What it can & can't recover](explainer-limits.qmd) |
| **Correctness** | How do you test scientific code that has no closed-form "right answer"? The oracle ladder and the meta-lessons. | [How we know it's right](explainer-testing.qmd) |

## Five ideas, if you read nothing else

1. **The adaptive kernel is a perplexity normaliser.** Each point gets a fixed
   *effective* number of fuzzy neighbours (`log₂ M`), so the bandwidth `σ`
   self-adapts to local density — dense regions get a sharp kernel, sparse ones
   a broad kernel. ([kernel](explainer-kernel.qmd))

2. **The continuous driver is the smoothest non-trivial coordinate on the
   recurrence graph** — the Fiedler eigenvector of the Laplacian, which
   minimises `Σ A_ij (f_i − f_j)²`. ([spectral](explainer-spectral.qmd))

3. **Consensus is a soft intersection.** Averaging fuzzy graphs keeps an edge
   only where many responses agree; spurious edges dilute as you add data, and
   the graph undergoes a *percolation transition* from one giant blob into
   driver-state basins. ([consensus](explainer-consensus.qmd))

4. **SHREC recovers the driver only up to a monotone transform**, and only the
   structure that *binary recurrence* can encode — which is why a 2-level driver
   is recovered near-perfectly but a 4-level one collapses to a 2-way split.
   ([limits](explainer-limits.qmd))

5. **You test it by triangulating** closed-form oracles, invariances, reference
   implementations, and statistical nulls — and by being honest when the truth
   is a limit, a convention, or a regime you had to find.
   ([testing](explainer-testing.qmd))

## A recurring meta-lesson

The same habit shows up at every stage: **localise a claim to the right
construction, triangulate the spec before trusting or "fixing" it, and let the
test track the truth** — including when that truth is uncomfortable (a method
that fails on period-4, a "fix" that lowers a sanity metric, a percolation curve
that only appears in the right coupling regime). Several of the pages below are
case studies in exactly that.
